Cross-examination by MR MYERS
My Lord, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: [Nurse B], you've explained that you took over the care of [Baby G] at about 11.30 on 21 September.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Could I ask you to keep your voice up if you could, please? I know it's a big room.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can I ask, was the reason for that that Ms Letby had been caring for a number of babies so the staffing was changed to try to lighten that workload at that point?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: I believe it was due to workload, but I was following shift leader instructions from Caroline Bennion.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All right. Thank you. As to the events as we go through the afternoon, [Baby G] had had to be fitted with a cannula, hadn't she, to receive the treatment she needed? She had a cannula when she came to you, didn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: She did.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you. And during the afternoon it was noted that the cannula wasn't working; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Well, the cannula was put in during the morning under Lucy's care. It may have been removed prior to me taking over, but she was certainly trying to be fitted with a working cannula when I took over.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you. As we get into the afternoon, the doctors then had to re-site the cannula; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And the first doctor who attempted to do that was Dr Chang, is that right, from what you can recall?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: I don't recall Dr Chang doing it under my watch, but from records, it shows she was the first one, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But she was unable to re-site it, wasn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And so Dr Harkness and Dr Gibbs both attended to deal with the cannulation of [Baby G], didn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: They did.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That cannulation took place in nursery 4, didn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And by your recollection, there were maybe a total of three babies in that room?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Maybe more. It was a busy room.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: A busy room. And there were parents in the room as well at points, weren't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As it happens, although you had been given [Baby G] to look after, you also had a baby in nursery 1, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: I don't remember being in nursery 1, but I definitely had a workload elsewhere.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And so is that why you were coming and going from the room as the cannulation went on?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The screens are put up -- as you have described to us, they go around the process, don't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Portable screen, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Portable screens. And when the cannulation took place, [Baby G] was put or placed on what's called a procedure trolley, wasn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: She was.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And a difference between that and a cot is the procedure trolley doesn't have sides, does it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: It does have sides, but not to the extent of -- it's not a sleeping facility.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All right, thank you. It's just one that's used temporarily when, as it says, there is a procedure to be performed; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: That's right, yes. You wouldn't leave a baby unattended on it because it does not have secure sides. The sides are able to be brought down, so the doctors or nurses performing the procedure can access a limb, for instance, for a cannula.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you. It seemed to take a little time for the cannulation to be performed successfully, didn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And there were multiple attempts by Dr Harkness and Dr Gibbs working together, weren't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: I believe it was Dr Gibbs attending to the cannula and Dr Harkness assisting, but they were certainly working together, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All right. And from what you know, did it take multiple attempts to site the cannula?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: It did.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: At the conclusion of a process like that, what should happen when the doctors are finished is that the screens are removed? That's what should happen?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The baby should be replaced back in the cot?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And then one or other of the doctors come and tell the designated nurse, or someone, that the process has been completed?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As it happened, the first that you knew that there was any issue with [Baby G] was when Lucy Letby called for help?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And when she called, is that when you then went into the nursery?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: I went -- I answered the call for help, I went to the doorway, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you. And you could see that [Baby G] was not the correct colour?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Was she a dusky colour or can you not remember?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: I cannot remember the exact colour. I remember her looking poorly.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: [Baby G] was struggling to breathe?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: She wasn't breathing.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She wasn't breathing. You could see that Ms Letby, Nurse Letby, was obviously concerned by what was taking place, wasn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: She was concerned, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And she was responding appropriately as far as you could see?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: As far as I could see, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The monitor was not on, was it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: The monitor was not on.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And you're not sure in fact whether it was attached; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: I'm unsure whether the probe was attached. The monitor was not on.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Right. Do you recall whether [Baby G] had been put back in the cot by this point or do you not know?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: She was in the cot.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She was in the cot. And we talked about the screens yesterday. Do you recall whether they'd actually been pushed back a bit or, from your recollection, were they in the same position?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Possibly, I just remember it still being there.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All right. I just want to deal with events later that afternoon. You explained to us yesterday, I've got the note of how the evidence was, that you contacted the police about a month ago, is that right, [Nurse B]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you. And you did that after you'd read the opening speeches online?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And it had seemed or you'd seen that it was suggested that Lucy Letby had turned the monitor off?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And from what happened, and we're going to come to that, you knew that wasn't the case?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: As far as I am aware, I believed that was not the case.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Right. When you say as far as you're aware, that's because this is what happened, isn't it? Later that day, Dr Gibbs and Dr Harkness came to you, didn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: They came to me.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And they spoke to you in the corridor outside nursery 4?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Your belief was they must be coming to you because you had mentioned to Eirian Powell that the monitor had been switched off. That's what you thought had happened; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: I can't remember the order, whether I spoke to Eirian Powell first, or Dr Harkness and Dr Gibbs came to me.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In any event, you can't remember which one it was who spoke or whether both of them spoke, you can't remember that precisely?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But you do recall they were both present when this conversation took place?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Both of them were very apologetic, weren't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: They were.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And they were apologetic because, as they explained, they hadn't told you they had finished with [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And apologetic because they hadn't switched the monitor back on?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And apologetic because they had left [Baby G] behind the screen?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And as you have explained to us, the nurse, or a person, should have been told when they left, shouldn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Someone, ideally the nurse allocated to them.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And certainly she should not have been left behind a screen, should she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And the monitor should have been turned back on?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: It should.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In fact the reason that you discovered where [Baby G] was and what was happening was because Nurse Letby had called out for help?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: She had.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: After that, after the incident where you had gone to Nurse Letby because she'd called for you --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- I'm just going back in time a little bit -- afterwards did she talk to you about finding [Baby G] there; do you recall that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: I don't recall that conversation.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All right. I'm just going to ask you a few things about what I'm going to suggest happened, but you say if you recall it or if it didn't happen.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Okay.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Was she cross that the doctors had left her behind the screen with the monitor off; do you remember that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: I don't remember that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You don't.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: I remember her being concerned for [Baby G]'s welfare.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you. Do you recall whether she had said, "Maybe this is something to make a complaint about", a formal complaint?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: I don't remember, but I did go to my manager to report it myself without anyone else suggesting.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Again, agree or disagree as you see fit, [Nurse B], but did she raise the prospect of putting a report on what's called the Datix system because of [Baby G] being left like that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: I don't recall.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Could she have said that and you just don't recall?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: It's highly likely.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, I think that's an interesting proposition. Do you recall any such conversation?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: NURSE B: No.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Well, why do you say it's highly likely then?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Because that's the reporting system of an incident.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I remember reporting to my manager directly. So whether the incident has been reported from my manager on to a Datix, I don't know. I didn't complete the Datix myself.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You didn't do one yourself?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: NURSE B: No, I didn't.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And you don't know whether anyone else did?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm grateful, my Lord. There's a subsidiary question that goes with that that may knit that together.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: What I was going to ask was this, [Nurse B]: was there a conversation where Ms Letby explained what had happened and raised an issue with it and you said to her you would deal with it your way? Do you recall saying something like that, that you'd speak to someone about it?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: No, I don't.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And I will ask, was there any aspect of you being anxious at all about raising a complaint then about what the consultants had done or not?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: I reported it to my manager as soon as [Baby G] was stabilised in nursery 1. I didn't delay, I reported it on exactly the same day.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And do you recall who it was in terms of your manager who you reported it to? Do you know who that was?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Eirian Powell.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Right. Well, thank you very much for dealing with that, [Nurse B].

Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, it's a statement from Valerie Thomas, returning to the chronology. She signs her statement on 19 March 2020 and she says as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Prior to this interview, I have reviewed the relevant medical notes concerning [Baby G], who was born at Arrowe Park Hospital on 31 May 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "In 2015 I was a full-time nursery nurse on the NNU at the Countess of Chester Hospital, predominantly working in special care rooms 3 and 4 within the NNU.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Referring to 21 September 2015, I have reviewed my medical notes and rotas from 16 September 2015. I was working a night shift, that's 19.30 hours to 08.00 hours, beginning on 20 September 2015, going through into 21 September.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My first entry on the medical notes that relate to [Baby G] is timed at 07.24 on 21 September. The notes do not say which nursery room [Baby G] was in. [Baby G]'s observations were satisfactory. Her temperature was 36.4 to 36.7. 36.4 is a little low, but she was well wrapped up, being nursed in a cot. [Baby G] was still on three-hourly feeds. She was completing her own bottles, but she had one nasogastric tube at 3 o'clock to rest.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G] settled after the 21.15 feed that her father gave her. She passed urine and had her bowels open.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: She had her medication as prescribed by the neonatal staff. At 6 am, 06.00 hours, I took routine bloods that morning from [Baby G]. [Baby G] was due for immunisation that day. At 08.00 hours that day I went off duty."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR RACHEL CHANG (read)

My Lord, it's slightly out of turn, but I turn next, please, to Rachel Chang who, we heard a moment ago from [Nurse B], was involved in treatment on the day of the 21st and whose notes we'll look at in due course with a different doctor. If I could read her statement now also.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is a statement dated 30 April 2018. Dr Chang says as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "In September 2015 I was an ST3 in paediatrics posted for 6 months as a registrar in the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "This was my first post as a senior doctor. My role at that time was to oversee and cover all children under the age of 16 and those who were under 18 with mental health problems who come into the Countess of Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would be split between the neonatal unit (NNU), accident and emergency, deliveries, or the children's ward depending on the rota.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "In reference to 21 September 2015, from memory I cannot remember anything about this particular date, the NNU unit or anything in reference to [Baby G]. From the notes I have written, I would have started my duties at 08.30, possibly ending either 17.00 or 18.00. However, if I was on call it could have ended at 21.00.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G], on 16 September 2015, was returned from Arrowe Park Hospital physically stable. On 21 September 2015, it appears senior house officer Dr Peter Fielding was doing a ward round when [Baby G] had had a large vomit and went tachycardic. Dr Fielding has been asked to review [Baby G]. At this stage Lucy Letby is the designated nurse for [Baby G].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "In Dr Fielding's notes, made at 10.30 am, he states that [Baby G] had an episode at 10.20 am. The nurses called for help. Dr Fielding goes to [Baby G], who was by that time recovered. He examines [Baby G], documenting that she had a low temperature and that her tummy was distended.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: There is a mention from the nurses that this is 'normal for [Baby G]'. Dr Fielding has then discussed [Baby G]'s condition with me, possibly by telephone. I have suggested to aspirate the nasogastric tube and 'leave on free drainage', the idea being to empty [Baby G]'s stomach of any air that may be causing the distension, and I suggested delaying the next feed, monitoring [Baby G]'s stomach and testing [Baby G]'s blood via a heel prick.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 11.50 am, I have documented that I have reviewed [Baby G], saying that she is pale, tachycardic, with a heart rate up to 190 beats per minute, had one feed delayed, and had no further vomiting. I documented that according to nursing staff and parents that 'she is not herself'. On examining her she was self-ventilating in air, had good oxygen levels, and her heart rate had settled to 160 to 170. I mentioned she is quieter than normal. With regards to her distended tummy, I have said that she is soft and distended, so I have recommended for partial screening for sepsis. Dr Gibbs is mentioned as having reviewed [Baby G]'s condition and recommended a broad spectrum antibiotic called cefotaxime.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "A temporary cannula was fitted at this point into [Baby G], possibly by me, but I can't remember, in order to get samples so we could check for bugs in her bloodstream. This was also used to administer antibiotics and 10% dextrose intravenously into [Baby G].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I would have been assisted by a nurse but I don't remember who. This line that I may have fitted has obviously failed at some
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: point. Dr Gibbs was called to assist in the fitting of the next cannula, possibly by me but I can't remember. It also documented that Dr Gibbs has recommended a suppository in case she is constipated.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "After being informed by somebody I can't remember, rather than being a witness to this episode, I have then made an entry at 15.30 saying that [Baby G] had a desaturation, requiring bagging (Neopuffing) due to poor respiratory effort.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Dr Fielding had noted that [Baby G] desaturated and her oxygen level went down to 30% and [Baby G] appeared to be apnoeic. The notes then say that by 15.30, Dr Gibbs inserted a cannula into [Baby G]'s left foot. This is usually after the initial one failing. I can't remember if I was present or not when Dr Gibbs fitted the cannula.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I made no further entries within the notes that day, which would suggest that I had nothing further to do with [Baby G] as in the nursing notes it appears she is stable and recovering. I cannot remember if any screens were around [Baby G] when the cannula process was taking place."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We'll stop there, please, and hopefully call Dr Fielding if he's here.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Ideally, it might have been better for Dr Fielding, who's referred to in that witness's evidence, to be called first. There's obviously an overlap between the two.

blocks.text: You noted that scans at Arrowe Park revealed mild dilation of the ventricles within her brain?

blocks.text: Yes, that's ultrasound scans in the early weeks of life.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And that you observed that mild ventricular dilation is not always associated with subsequent adverse developmental progress?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, it's difficult to prognosticate, to know the outcome from just ultrasound scans.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You summarised that she was stable during the first 3 weeks following her transfer from Arrowe Park.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And you note events on 7 September 2015, where she suddenly deteriorated, as you put it, with a profuse vomit.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, but I wasn't directly involved at that time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You had, as you indicate here, no direct involvement with [Baby G] on 7 September and she thereafter spent 9 days at Arrowe Park.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And you note that her blood C-reactive protein rose to 218 whilst at Arrowe Park.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We have heard that that was some time on 9 September, so 2 days after her transfer.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: She returned to Chester on 16 September. You summarise that over the next few days, the doctors who examined her recorded that she was stable and continuing to manage without any supplemental oxygen.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: On 20 September, you note that [Dr C], your consultant colleague, had a conversation with [Baby G]'s parents about the results of an MRI scan.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct, yes, a brain scan.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. And ischaemic changes were noted to the brain?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Brought about by the lack of blood and oxygen reaching parts of the brain in that particular case?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You first became directly involved with [Baby G] on 21 September; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think you were consultant of the week.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'd started -- at the beginning of the week it was a Monday and I had started as consultant of the week, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And that gave you, did it, responsibility for the care of the patients on the NNU during the daytime?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you have any direct recollection of the events of 21 September?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Only a vague recollection. Most of my recollection is from reviewing the medical notes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did you or were you present during any collapse that [Baby G] suffered on that day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As far as I can recall, I was present after her collapse in the morning. You have heard from Dr Fielding, who was
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: immediately summoned when she first had the vomiting in the morning, and then a registrar, Dr Chang, attended to [Baby G], and I went to the unit, as is normal practice.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: After doing the ward round on the paediatric ward, the normal practice each day is to go to the neonatal unit, which is when I became involved with [Baby G] at that time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In your witness statement you have noted that from his(?) notes that a fall to 30% by way of desaturation is a significant event.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's a severe desaturation, drop in oxygen level.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You have recited, and I'm not going to do it with you because we, as you rightly point out, have just looked at it. You recite the content of Dr Fielding's notes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So you had those in mind presumably when you saw [Baby G] later in the day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, and particularly Dr Chang, the registrar, who had seen [Baby G] as well.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Dr Chang's notes are available. Perhaps if we can go to those, please. Tile 57.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we can look at the notes. That's the end of Dr Fielding's, but we have an entry at 11.50 from Dr Chang which I think you -would you have seen this when you attended [Baby G] that day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Likely to have but certainly that would have been discussed with me.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think if we just scroll -- I will just give you an opportunity to look at it, please, to refresh your memory from that particular day and ask you if anything stands out to you in that particular entry.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, Dr Chang is being asked to see because [Baby G]'s heart rate had increased and she was looking pale, but before that she had had some projectile profuse vomiting that Dr Fielding has recorded, and yet the encouraging fact is when it says "resp" in the left margin, that's respiratory, she's remaining in air, that's spontaneous ventilation in air, SVIA, and her saturations, oxygen levels, were good at 94% to 96%, so that was reassuring, that given she's a vulnerable premature baby with chronic lung disease, despite the problems she'd had that morning, her breathing was satisfactory.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And the CRT at the bottom is just capillary refill time, an estimate of circulation and it says less than 2 seconds. That's reassuring as well at the time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: There's an entry there about heart rate. Tell us about that, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's faster than usual. It should be up to 170 to 180 but that's a little high.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But it would appear that it settled after that initial --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. And other indicators I have mentioned were encouraging.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Can you just scroll through the rest of that entry, please. Again these are the notes which you would have been familiar with on the day and that you refreshed your memory from. Is there anything there that stands out to you as a treating consultant?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The fact that [Baby G] had had a large vomit -- in fact, I think Dr Fielding recorded it as two large projectile vomits, and it's just unusual for a premature baby, who had been feeding entirely satisfactorily since returning from Arrowe Park Hospital, to actually have projectile vomiting.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Her abdomen is distended, but many premature babies, particularly like [Baby G], who have had a difficult time with ventilation for 5 weeks followed by needing continued support for some weeks for their breathing with CPAP and Optiflow administration of oxygen, it's not uncommon to have a slightly distended tummy because of the increased work of breathing over many weeks and the lax soft abdominal muscles that premature babies have. So [Baby G] had frequently quite a distended tummy.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If we scroll down the note, I think there may be a diagram of her tummy, which is described as soft.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It's distended but soft and good bowel sounds present.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The plan at 11.50, if we could just have a look at that, please, scroll down a little bit, Mr Murphy. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Certainly after the reference to a partial screen, it would seem you've been certainly involved to an extent following that examination. Could you tell us about that, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There would have been at least a discussion between Dr Chang and myself and one possibility for a baby who vomits and who is looking quieter, more pale than usual, is they might have an infection and we tend to cover for infections first because it's serious if we delay treatment for infections. So the plan for [Baby G] at that time was to do a partial screen and that means to check for infection, but "partial" means to omit a lumbar puncture because that's quite an invasive, traumatic procedure. It involves curling a baby up into a C shape to expose their back and stick a needle in and with someone like [Baby G], who had had a lot of problems with her breathing, that could compromise her breathing. So we weren't going to do a lumbar puncture but we did do blood tests and the blood culture and started an antibiotic.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is that the reference to --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- cefotaxime?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It says "reviewed", which means I would have seen Paige (sic), so:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Dr Gibbs reviewed. For cefotaxime only currently."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Now, if she'd suffered from necrotising enterocolitis, which has been discussed with other babies before, if she was suffering from that we'd normally give several antibiotics. But I felt at that time -- I must have felt at that time that she was unlikely to have necrotising enterocolitis, and so we were only covering for other infections at that stage.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then you move on to agree a plan with Dr Chang. Tell us about that, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. [Baby G] at that time didn't have intravenous access, didn't have a cannula, she'd needed that at various times in the past, but because she'd been feeding well and stable, she didn't have intravenous access but because she'd had this vomit or several projectile vomits and then had been quieter than usual and then had a temporary increased heart rate, we were covering for infections, so the plan was not to feed her into her tummy at that, stage to give her intravenous fluids and intravenous antibiotics, but to do an abdominal Xray, looking for other complications, particularly necrotising enterocolitis signs on the X-ray.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But also she -- [Baby G] had also suffered from constipation and was on lactulose, a laxative, for her constipation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And I wondered -- I think at this stage I must have seen the abdominal X-ray. I can't now recall the actual abdominal X-ray, but I suggested she has a suppository as well. Because her tummy was distended and because the X-ray -- it's recorded somewhere — yes, so stools in the rectum, it's written there by Dr Chang, I wondered whether she was a little bunged up at the bottom end and that was adding to her abdominal distension, so a suppository might help her.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. We can go, I think, to tile 60, if that's possible, and look at the X-ray if that assists.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Let's check the time and the date on the X-ray before I ask you if it's... Can we scroll down a little bit, Mr Murphy? So that's at 12.21 on the 21st, so about half an hour after Dr Chang began making her note.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So does that -- can you confirm that's the X-ray that you'd have looked at?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's likely to have been, yes, because it showed a bowel filled with air, with gas, and that's what this X-ray shows. Down the bottom end, so it's where the pelvis is at the bottom, it's more opaque, sort of just diffusely grey rather than that black gas appearance, which is what I assumed could have been faeces in her rectum, knowing that she suffered from constipation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That prompted the suggestion of a suppository to help, if that's right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You mentioned some bloods that were taken from -- blood tests taken from [Baby G].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If we can go next, please, to tile 59, and look at the document. We can see [Baby G]'s name in the top left, collection at 12.17. Tell us what the result of that blood test tells us, please, or tells you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This blood test collected on the 21st, it's several days later and the date when it was authorised, the report is the 27th, but after several days the bottom line says:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Culture: no bacterial growth after 5 days of incubation."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So at the time when we're suspecting infection we usually can't tell from blood tests immediately that there is a bacterial infection present. We take the blood, it has to be incubated in a laboratory for several days. We usually get a report back within 48 hours from the laboratory, but the final report is after 5 days and this report shows that no bacterial infection was grown from [Baby G]'s blood at that time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So what does that tell you about the possibility of infection?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It lowers the possibility of infection, it doesn't rule it out because premature babies can suffer from infection without always showing a positive blood culture.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. If we go back to our sequence of events chart and look at tile 67. If we can look at the results, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We can see again [Baby G]'s name towards the top left-hand side of the form and confirming that the collection date for that was 21 September. If we scroll down, please, there are a number of results shown. What are you able to tell us, please, about those results, Dr Gibbs?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The first few results there, the sodium, potassium, urea, are showing the electrolytes in the blood. The sodium is at the low end of normal, but we knew from various treatments [Baby G] had had, she'd been on diuretic treatment to help her chronic lung disease, that does tend to drop the sodium, but those are satisfactory results.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The most relevant abnormal result, which has the H next to it, is the CRP level, which is 18. It should be less than 10. That would suggest she could have an infection. But it has to be taken in the context of the fact that we knew, just under 2 weeks earlier, her CRP level had been 218 and I couldn't be sure at this stage whether this is a new rise in the CRP level or just the previous high CRP level actually still falling.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We hadn't had a CRP checked on [Baby G] since she'd come back to the Countess of Chester 5 days earlier.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. So was this when you had spoken earlier about putting [Baby G] on that first line of antibiotics?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Were these the kind of results that you were balancing in that decision?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We can scroll down the rest of that document, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Unfortunately, the blood sample that was sent for the full blood count, looking at the white cell count and the haemoglobin level, had clotted, and so there was no results available. But I think later in the day we did get a full blood count.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right, okay. I'm going to move on, please, in the day to about 3.30 that afternoon and tile 75. This is another note by Dr Chang in which you are involved. So I'm going to ask Mr Murphy if we can scroll down again, please, and you have an opportunity to look at what's been noted.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)

Dr Chang here is recording that -- she's recording at 3.30 in the afternoon that [Baby G] had had a desaturation, not quite as low as in the morning, down to 50%, still a very significant drop, and in fact required some bagging. That just means temporary ventilation support because she was showing a poor respiratory effort at that stage.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Now, I can't recall whether I was there with [Baby G] at the time that happened. What Dr Chang is noting then is that I had inserted a cannula into [Baby G]'s left foot and I can't remember whether, having inserted that cannula, I was still there when [Baby G] had this desaturation or whether I'd left the unit by that stage, but I'd been there recently and inserted a cannula.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What can you remember of the occasion that afternoon when you fitted the cannula to [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember much, 7 years ago, what happened during the cannula insertion. [Baby G], like any other premature baby, who was by then 4 months old and had had lot of intensive care treatment in the early weeks or the first few months of her life, would have by that stage been very difficult to insert a cannula into because most of her veins would have been used for cannulation. So it was difficult to find a vein to insert a
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: cannula and I believe that I was the last of several people who tried to insert a cannula that day into [Baby G].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Do you remember whether anyone was with you when you were attempting to fit that cannula?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember who specifically was with me. It would normally be the nurse or nurses looking after [Baby G].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you remember what room you were in when you fitted that particular cannula?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, sorry. I know that subsequently, the hospital notes say -- medical notes say that [Baby G] was then moved into the intensive care room, nursery 1, so she was in one of the outside nursery rooms, but I don't remember which one.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You can eliminate number 1 based on the notes, but you don't know --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I can't remember which one she was in.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You told us it's difficult, with a baby like [Baby G], to cannulate given her history. Can you remember whether you tried more than one location to cannulate her?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I can't remember, but given that several people tried, various locations would have been tried.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you recall where or what type of bed, if that's the right word, [Baby G] was in or on at the time you were cannulating her?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I can't remember. It's likely to have been a cot, but I can't remember what bed she was in. Sometimes babies are moved on to an open cot, which just means the sides can be lowered to gain access to their limbs more easily to insert a cannula. But I can't remember on this particular day what sort of cot [Baby G] was in when I was trying to put the cannula in.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We've heard about a trolley, which is a flat surface, which can be used sometimes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's the open cot I meant.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But no recollection which it was?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember, no, back 7 years.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Do you remember, once you had successfully fitted the cannula, what you then did?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you remember whether there were screens around [Baby G] at the time you were fitting the cannula?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I can't remember whether there were screens.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I mean, if other babies had been in the room, and particularly other parents sitting with their babies, then screens are often put up, just to shield the baby undergoing a procedure from other parents. But I can't remember on this day whether there were any screens up.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you remember whether [Baby G] was connected to an alarm or monitor of any sort?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, she should have been because, given her problems, given she'd come back from having needed to be ventilated again from Arrowe Park Hospital just 5 days earlier, she should have been on monitoring, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Having ruled out room 1 as the location, does that assist you with the type of monitor that [Baby G] would have been connected to?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't recall on this day exactly what monitor she was attached to but she was likely to have had had an oxygen saturation monitor attached to her.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And how are they attached to the baby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The probe that detects -- the little light from the probe that detects the oxygen level through the skin is either wrapped round a foot, a hand or sometimes the earlobe. And it can be moved around.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We've heard it referred to as a Masimo monitor.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is that the type that -- are you describing the same --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- type of device?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And when you are attempting different locations with a cannula, does, from time to time, the sensor need to be moved?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it does because if you're trying to cannulate, say the foot or the hand, and the monitor is wrapped around that foot or hand, you have to take it off.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Are you able to recall whether you had to do that on this occasion?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did you, as a matter of course, have a protocol or a routine when that situation arose?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We didn't have a fixed protocol, written protocol, to follow. But if a monitor is taken off because you need access to a part of a baby for a procedure, then it should be applied to some other part of the body, so you would move it from one hand to the other or one leg to the other. I could either do it myself or the nurse looking after the baby would do it.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Would the monitor ever be removed altogether?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There shouldn't be no monitoring at all.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Are there occasions you can think of when it has been -- for example, the sensor's been left on the mattress or taken away from the baby for some reason?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, if that does happen it should be very temporary, unless there's some other form of monitoring. Now, the babies in the outside rooms in the neonatal unit can have an apnoea monitor as well and I don't remember whether [Baby G] had an apnoea monitor. But if she had some other form of monitoring then the oxygen saturation monitor may be left off for a while as long as there's some other monitor attached to [Baby G].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If it's just a Masimo monitor?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It shouldn't be left off, no.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Shouldn't be left disconnected. Should it ever be switched off?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, if that's the only monitoring device for a baby.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And they were undergoing that monitoring at the time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Are there any circumstances when you have had to turn one off whilst cannulating a baby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember having to do that and I can't remember exactly what I did for [Baby G], but I know for babies I have
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: had to move the monitor, where it was attached to the baby, from one limb to another or asked the nurse looking after the baby to do that, but I can't remember in [Baby G]'s case exactly what we did with the monitor.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. You told us you can't remember what happened after you'd cannulated [Baby G].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What would your routine be once you'd successfully fitted the cannula?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, the cannula was needed for fluids and for antibiotics, so the nurses would have set those up.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I would have checked that [Baby G] was stable at the time, otherwise I wouldn't have left, which is why I'm not sure that I was there when she had this desaturation and needed to be bagged.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So what would checking [Baby G] was stable have involved before you left her after cannulation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Firstly, just looking at a baby to make sure she was breathing regularly and her colour looked normal and if the monitor was attached, which it should be, that the monitor was giving a satisfactory reading.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If you weren't fitting the cannula with the nurse, would you need to alert anybody once you'd finished?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, I wouldn't have just left [Baby G] by herself without telling anyone. Yes, I would have had to tell someone.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Who would you ordinarily tell once it was fitted?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Whichever nurse was looking after [Baby G] if they were still on the unit. They might have been off on a break, so one of other nurses. But it's usually when you're undertaking a procedure like trying to insert a cannula that the nurse would still be around.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So if not the nurse, the designated nurse, then whoever -- whichever nurse was available?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, one of the other nurses looking after babies, and ideally in that same room.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But I have to admit I can't remember exactly who I told and what I did at the time [Baby G] had her cannula.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. You can't remember leaving [Baby G]. Do you recall having any conversation with anyone on the unit after you'd left [Baby G] about the cannulation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I can't remember having such a conversation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We've heard that Eirian Powell was, I think, in charge of the unit on that particular day. Did you have any conversation with her that you can recall about cannulation or monitors or anything of that sort?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember that conversation, no.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you recall any conversation with -- we have heard that [Baby G]'s designated nurse was [Nurse B].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You know [Nurse B], I assume?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I do know her, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you remember any conversation with [Nurse B] after you had cannulated -- any relevant conversation after you'd cannulated [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember that now. If it had been a significant discussion then usually the staff nurse would have recorded that in the nursing notes if there'd been a worry about the procedure, some concern about it.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Which nurse would have entered that in the nursing notes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, if there was a nurse, which I thought there would have been, attending to [Baby G] at the time I was trying to cannulate her, or if there wasn't one there at the time, whichever nurse I had spoken to after I'd finished the cannulation. But I can't remember who that was.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In your experience, the type of thing that would be noted in the nursing notes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If there was some concern that something wrong had happened or there had been some worry. But if I'd been particularly concerned I should have recorded it in the medical notes and I didn't.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. I'm going to go back to tile 75, please. We're on 75. Go back to 71, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is the line insertion and removal record chart.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm sure you'll recognise it. Is that your signature or is that your handwriting on the form?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. Someone else has written that. They've put my name there, but someone else has written it.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That indicates it's a peripheral IV, fitted to the left foot by yourself, and that's the 7th attempt by multiple staff, which echoes, I think, what you were telling us earlier.

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: Nursery 2, which is designated high dependency, there's Caroline Oakley looking after two babies, NC and AC, isn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: You were designated to look after RH, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As it appears on there, yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: As it appears there. And Janet Cox, a baby designated IH; yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: Were you the shift leader on this shift?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I was.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: In nursery 3 there are two babies, IO and a baby called [Baby I], and Janet Cox was the nurse for both of them, wasn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: Was she a band 4 nurse, Janet Cox?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: And nursery 4, where [Baby G] was with two other babies, Lucy Letby was the designated nurse there, wasn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: And also you can see a box at the bottom right saying "Baby whose location is unconfirmed". Do you recall that there was another baby who you were or may have been looking after at this time, AO?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I don't.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: Earlier in the case we considered, and we may have considered with you in fact, about what the staffing levels are for looking after babies in the nurseries.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: Just to refresh us, though we may not have forgotten, it's meant to be one-to-one for intensive care babies, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: And those nurses have to be intensive care trained, don't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: For high dependency, one nurse can look after up to two babies; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: And in special care one nurse can look after up to four?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: Ideally, the shift leader should be what's been described as supernumerary, in other words able to move anywhere, but not designated to any particular child; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. Ideally. Or if they are -- if they do have a patient workload it's a lighter patient workload.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: If we look at the number of babies, there appear to be 13 or possibly 14, depending what the position with OR was. Thirteen with six staff, including you. That's staff stretched, let me put it this way, very, very tightly over a lot of obligations, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, if you've got special care babies, it's one to four. So actually six staff... Um... That's actually quite -that's within BAPM guidelines, which were set in 2011. So actually one nurse, or nursery nurse, is looking after four -is capable of looking after four patients, so -- and although actually some of those babies, it doesn't actually give us the ratio of whether they are special care, high dependency in 2, 3 or 4 on there either. Presuming that nursery 3 and 4 are special care babies, that's an appropriate workload.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: Yes. If we get to nursery 1, if they are intensive care babies in there, then ideally it should be one-to-one, shouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Ideally it should be one to one.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: And ideally if [Baby G] was redesignated to [Nurse B], that would take [Nurse B] outside the BAPM guidelines, at that point, wouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It would slightly. However, you've got another registered member of staff in there, so you've got two members of staff to support each other within there, so it wouldn't be as if [Nurse B] would be on her own in there, she's got another band 5 nurse, and [Nurse B] is a very senior band 6 nurse.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: I'm just looking at it alongside the guidelines and on the guidelines if there are intensive care babies it should be one to one, shouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Ideally it should be.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: And in fact, as we've seen in the notes, the reason that [Baby G] was transferred to [Nurse B] was sheer staff workload where Lucy Letby was concerned, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And also reallocation of nurseries. So if [Baby G] needed to move from nursery 4 to nursery 1, that made sense for [Nurse B] who had the smallest workload to resume care of [Baby G].
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: As it happens, we know [Baby G] wasn't moved to nursery '1 until after the second event.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: So at the time that [Baby G] was reallocated to [Nurse B] she wasn't in the process of being moved, was she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It was a few hours later, yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: And after the cannulation and the desaturation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: In any event, the workload was at least a factor in why [Baby G] was redesignated to [Nurse B]; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It was, yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: So far as you're aware from what we see, what happened in event 1 was relatively brief and there appears to have been a swift recovery afterwards, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The first event was.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: Yes. Do you recall saying to the police you wouldn't describe the event at 10.15 as a collapse, more as a significant event due to [Baby G] self-resolving?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, correct.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: So not a collapse, a significant event due to selfresolving?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: And just this in conclusion where [Baby G] is concerned, Mrs Bennion: she was, in your view, a risk-vulnerable baby, wasn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: Who did have the potential to deteriorate as she did?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All our babies have got the potential, that's why they're closely monitored, to deteriorate, yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: That's right, isn't it? A neonatal unit is for close monitoring for babies who have the potential to deteriorate, don't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: And it's something you commented on, that [Baby G] had the potential to deteriorate in the way that she did; do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, because she was an extremely premature baby, who although was doing well, did have the potential at any stage to deteriorate.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: All right. Thank you, Mrs Bennion.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Does your Lordship have any questions?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I don't, thank you very much.

blocks.text: Of course.

blocks.text: Thank you very much indeed.

blocks.text: MRS EIRIAN POWELL (affirmed)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Could we begin with your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's Eirian Lloyd Powell.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Is it Miss or Mrs Powell?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mrs.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Were you employed at the Countess of Chester Hospital in September of 2015?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: In what capacity, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As the neonatal manager.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Thank you. You have come here today to deal with events on 21 September 2015 and you know that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: And also to answer any questions about [Baby G] that anyone may have, a baby called [Baby G].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: If we begin at the beginning. Do you remember [Baby G] from your own recollections?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I don't, actually.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Okay. In respect of 21 September, have you had the opportunity to check the notes that would have been made at the time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I have. I was currently off sick until the 21st, where -- on the 21st, I'd returned on a phased return after fracturing my leg.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: So it's a day you remember?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: A phased return, what does that mean?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It means you start off with a few hours initially and you build up on it, which is agreed with your superior manager.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: So do you remember what shift you were pencilled in for on 21 September?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Looking at the -- it looks like I was doing a 5.5hour, according to the diary.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Okay. What time, do you remember, did you come on duty?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember what time I actually came on duty, but I was supposed to leave at 1, so working back, I must have come on about 7.30.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Right. So if it was a 5.5-hour shift and assuming you finished at 1, you have worked out you probably started at 7.30?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: And did you leave at 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember if I did.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: What would your duties have entailed then in the neonatal unit on that particular day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, I was asked to -- I'd got in my diary that I had [Baby G]'s immunisations to do that morning, so I went round to -- I always check to make sure that they're sufficiently stable to have the immunisations because they can compromise the babies' well-being. There was some instability with the temperatures, so I was told that she wasn't well enough at that time to have the immunisations and therefore they were withheld.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Do you remember roughly what stage of your shift or what time of the day that conversation took place?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I don't.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Do you remember who it took place with?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't know. I'd be guessing.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: We don't want you to guess. If you don't remember, please say so.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay, so your shift, as you recall it to be, the whole of that shift would have been spent within the NNU?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not necessarily. I mean, there would be a return to work with my immediate manager at some point. Again I don't remember what time that would have been. And it would be trying to catch up, really, with what I'd been off...
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Did you have any meetings outside of the unit on that particular --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It said I had a specialty meeting at 12.00. I don't remember.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: How long would that be?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That would be from 12 o'clock to 1.30, 2 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Okay. That would take you beyond the end of your shift, as you recall it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Okay. Do you happen to remember if you returned to the NNU after the meeting?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember. I can't even remember if I went to the meeting.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I can't.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: That certainly makes that clear. You told us that you recall going on to the unit and having a conversation about [Baby G]'s immunisations due that day.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Did you have any other conversations that you remember about [Baby G] or her treatment?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: No?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Any conversations with anybody about events that could be described as untoward on the unit that day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. How do you mean, untoward?
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: It's a term that is used in your witness statement, so I've been very careful to use that. Whatever interpretation you put on that, anything that seemed incorrect, anything wrong on the unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, there wasn't anything, no.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: What was the process -- if an incident that you did consider to be untoward had taken place, what was your responsibility as a manager on the unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, it would be reported to me directly or Yvonne, my deputy, and I would be dealing with that directly. It depends on what actually it entails because if it was a performance issue, it would be Datix-ed, as in a clinical incident would be reported. But if it was something personal or something that could be resolved with talking to that person directly or requiring additional supervision, then that could be done from that point in time.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Okay. So in a management role --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: -- rather than a more formal role, would that be fair to say?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: When you describe an incident as a clinical incident requiring a Datix form, is it required in the event of a clinical incident?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What?
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: A Datix report.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: In the clinical --
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Is it mandatory --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, yes. Anything that's not followed procedure, a clinical incident would actually be done and anyone can do that.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Okay (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It doesn't have to go through me. But I usually get a copy of that incident reporting.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Okay. You may have just helped with one form of incident where you said failing to follow procedure.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: I'm just wondering what you meant, for those laypersons amongst us, by a clinical incident. What definition would you give to those matters that required reporting on Datix?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, it's as wide as it's long. It can be absolutely anything from not giving a medication within a given time, with omitting or failure to give, withholding, or even -- well, for instance, if you have to cannulate an infant more than three times.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's usually considered as an incident. Not always done, because sometimes it's not possible to do, you know... From the natural... They're very difficult to cannulate and when they're poorly it's even harder because they do actually -- I'm going to use this terminology now -- shut down --
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- where the vessels are not easy to access, so it's even harder. So you know, it can be difficult to cannulate.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Okay. Picking up something you said, another thing you said a moment ago, it doesn't have to be you that makes the Datix report?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Can it be any member of staff?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Anybody can do it.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: And can it relate to an omission or a failure by any other member of staff regardless of their status?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. And we were very good at doing that, yes, as a collective.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Thank you, I have no more questions, Mrs Powell. If you could wait there for a moment, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Mrs Powell, can I pick up on what we were talking about there, just a couple of things. You say that if there was
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: an issue, sometimes it's a Datix report that would be lodged; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, which is the clinical incident.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: A clinical incident. And you gave the example of cannulation in fact, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: That if there's been three -- more than three times arguably that could be something that would be a Datix report?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: And if there were seven attempts --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: -- that could be as well, couldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: And it doesn't have to be any person in particular, does it, who makes the report?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, anyone can do it.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: So if a doctor, for example, had taken seven attempts to cannulate, he or she could choose to make a Datix report about it --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: -- or they might not?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but they could explain also in the clinical notes as to what the problem was.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: They could.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: There might be a number of ways of resolving issues that arise, would that be fair to say?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: One of the ways might be sometimes for someone to talk to someone about what had happened; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: And it may be that the view is taken that's a better way of resolving the issue that's arisen; do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, could you...?
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Maybe sometimes talking to someone about what happened might be a way of dealing with the issue --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: -- if I put it that way?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Do you actually remember the conversations that you had on 21 September? I'm not going to suggest you would, but do you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: And it sounds like it was the first day back after a bit of a break.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, literally.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: And there were a number of things that you'd have had to deal with that day?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: And do you remember any particular conversations about [Baby G] that day?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, only that I was to give the immunisations but I was told they didn't think she was well enough.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Do you remember any conversations about [Baby G] or any aspect of her treatment in the days that followed, any particular conversation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Again, because I was on a phased return I didn't -- I think I was in perhaps three times that week on a shortened shift.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: All right. And do you remember any particular issues raised as to her care over that period with you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: You just don't remember?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, not at all.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Do you have a lot of conversations with a lot of people?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I do, yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mrs Powell.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- so I had to have a point of reference --
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: So you'd expect one or the other?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POWELL

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Does my Lord have any questions?

blocks.text: Just so I understand, so if an untoward clinical event has occurred, what you understood to be an untoward clinical event occurred, you would anticipate learning of that event, either by it being reported in Datix --

blocks.text: -- in other words, or reported to you orally?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Right. Thank you very much.

blocks.text: That completes your evidence. I don't think you're...
